new_value: Antoine "Fats" Domino was born in New Orleans in 1928 and grew up in the Lower Ninth Ward. After his piano-driven records made him a star of early rock and roll he chose to stay in the old neighborhood, and in 1960 he built a modern split-level home at Caffin Avenue and Marais Street, a few blocks from where he was raised. The house at 1208 Caffin Avenue became a neighborhood landmark. Domino was rescued from it by boat during the flooding that followed Hurricane Katrina in 2005. He died in 2017. The house is closed to the public, and its street now also carries his name.
reason: PBS American Masters and Slate both date the house to 1960, so "in the 1960s" is tightened and unsourced phrasing from the Substack post is dropped.

new_value: James Moore, who recorded as Slim Harpo, was born in February 1924 at Lobdell in West Baton Rouge Parish. He worked as a longshoreman and construction laborer and played Baton Rouge bars before his recording career began in 1957 with "I'm a King Bee." "Rainin' in My Heart" (1961) and "Baby Scratch My Back" (1966) both reached the top five of the rhythm and blues chart, and the Rolling Stones, the Kinks and many others recorded his songs. He died of a heart attack in January 1970, aged 45 (the marker says 46), and is buried beside his parents in Mulatto Bend Cemetery. A state historical marker stands at U.S. 190 and South Mulatto Bend Road.
reason: Born February 1924 and died 31 January 1970 makes him 45, not 46; the marker text the row copied is internally inconsistent.

new_value: William Haney, a World War I veteran and Black businessman, turned a 1930s barbecue stand in Ferriday into Haney's Big House, a nightclub with a dance floor, a motel for performers and even a bus ticket counter. At its peak from 1940 to 1966 it was a stop on the Chitlin' Circuit, hosting Ray Charles, B.B. King, Big Joe Turner, Roy Brown and Irma Thomas. A young Jerry Lee Lewis and his cousin Jimmy Swaggart listened from the sidewalk, then tried the music at the piano. The club burned in 1966 and was not rebuilt. A town historical marker at North First and Greathouse streets, mapped here, tells the story.
reason: The marker at North First and Greathouse was erected by the town of Ferriday; the separate Blues Trail marker is about 0.2 miles away.

new_value: J.D. Miller began recording Cajun bands in 1946 and set up a simple studio in Crowley in 1947, first at home and then at his M&S Electric shop on North Parkerson Avenue. He went on to record nearly every south Louisiana style: Cajun, country, zydeco, swamp pop and, above all, the swamp blues of Lightnin' Slim and Slim Harpo, which he licensed to Excello Records. The legacy is mixed, since in the 1960s Miller also issued openly racist records. In 1964 he bought the former Ford dealership mapped here and put his studio upstairs; the building is now Crowley City Hall, with a museum of his equipment. His MasterTrak studio later hosted John Fogerty and Paul Simon.
reason: The mapped City Hall building is itself a studio site: Miller bought it in 1964 and ran his studio on the second floor; the unsupported "from 1957" Excello date is removed.

new_value: Alfred "Fred" Tate bought a bar on Mamou's Sixth Street on November 20, 1946, and it became a small-town headquarters for the Cajun revival. Tate helped bring back Mamou's Courir de Mardi Gras, and in the 1960s his friend Revon Reed began broadcasting Cajun music from the lounge on Saturday mornings in Louisiana French; accounts date the show to 1962 or to 1968. It still airs, now over KVPI in Ville Platte. After Fred died in 1992, his former wife Sue Vasseur, known as Tante Sue, remained the lounge's hostess until her death in 2025. Fred's opens on Saturday mornings, with a Cajun band and dancing from nine o'clock.

new_value: On March 26, 1974, more than eight thousand people filled Lafayette's Blackham Coliseum for A Tribute to Cajun Music, produced by Barry Ancelet and the staff of CODOFIL. There was deliberately no dance floor: the organizers wanted the crowd to sit and listen to Dennis McGee, Nathan Abshire, Marc Savoy, Clifton Chenier and Dewey Balfa. The night is remembered as a milestone for French Louisiana music. In 1976 the event moved outdoors to Girard Park, dancing was allowed, and it grew into a free festival now held each October. It was renamed Festivals Acadiens et Créoles in 2008 to recognize Creole musicians.
reason: The cited article does not say Dewey Balfa inspired the no-dancing format or that the event became a fall festival in 1976, so both claims are trimmed.

new_value: In 1982, worried that zydeco and Creole music were dying out, Black Creole residents of the Opelousas area staged a festival on a farm field at Plaisance, north of town, with the backing of the Southern Development Foundation. Accounts credit a citizens' group called the Treasures of Opelousas and a committee from Holy Ghost Catholic Church led by the Rev. Albert McKnight. About four hundred people came the first year. The event grew into one of the country's leading zydeco festivals and the foundation's main fundraiser. In 2016 it left the Plaisance field, mapped here, for the indoor Yambilee grounds in Opelousas, where it has been held since.
reason: The festival moved to the Yambilee grounds in 2016 and made that its permanent home in 2017; the write-up now gives the year and drops band names not found in the sources.

new_value: The C.J. Peete public housing development, built in Central City in 1939 and known to everyone as the Magnolia, became the best-known address in New Orleans hip-hop. Brothers Bryan "Baby" Williams and Ronald "Slim" Williams started Cash Money Records around 1991 and tied the label to the complex. Juvenile and Turk of the Hot Boys grew up there, and Juvenile's 1998 video for "Ha" showed it to the country. Soulja Slim began rapping here as Magnolia Slim in 1993, and bounce artist Magnolia Shorty carried its name. The City Council voted in 2007 to demolish the complex; the mixed-income Harmony Oaks development now stands on the site.

new_value: Swamp pop is the rhythm-and-blues-flavored rock and roll that south Louisiana teenagers made their own in the late 1950s and early 1960s, trading the Cajun accordion and fiddle for electric guitars and horns. Ville Platte, where radio station KVPI pushed the new records, was proclaimed the Swamp Pop Capital of the World by the Louisiana Legislature, and in 2010 this museum opened in the town's old train depot. It displays stage costumes, photographs, records and a wall of autographs, and explains why so many performers took stage names, as Bobby Charles Guidry did for "See You Later, Alligator."

new_value: Amédé Ardoin, a Creole accordionist and singer from the Eunice and Basile area, was one of the first Creole musicians to make records. Between 1929 and 1934 he cut 34 songs, some with the Cajun fiddler Dennis McGee, and their waltzes and two-steps became a foundation for both Cajun music and zydeco; Iry LeJeune and Clifton Chenier drew on them. After a beating from which he never recovered, Ardoin died in 1942 in the state hospital at Pineville and was buried in an unmarked grave. On March 11, 2018, this steel statue by Russell Whiting, showing him standing on his accordion with a lemon in his hand, was unveiled to bring him home symbolically.
